title: A Style-Based Generator Architecture for Generative Adversarial Networks
authors: Tero Karras, Samuli Laine, Timo Aila (NVIDIA)

blocks.html: A standard GAN generator is a black box: you feed in a random vector $z$ and a stack of layers turns it into an image. It works, but you get almost no control — you cannot say 'keep this face but change the hair', because every attribute is smeared across the whole input vector in tangled ways. StyleGAN re-architects the generator so that control and disentanglement fall out naturally.

The paper's striking claim is that you can leave the discriminator and the loss completely unchanged and get a huge leap in quality and controllability purely by redesigning how the generator consumes its latent code. Three ideas do the work: (1) a mapping network that transforms $z$ into an intermediate code $w$; (2) injecting $w$ as a style via AdaIN at every resolution of the synthesis network; and (3) adding explicit per-pixel noise for stochastic detail.

The payoff is dramatic. StyleGAN produced the photorealistic 1024x1024 faces that powered the famous 'thispersondoesnotexist' demo, and it does so while letting you mix the coarse structure of one face with the fine details of another — a level of control no prior GAN offered.

Underlying it all is a notion of disentanglement: the authors argue (and measure) that the intermediate space $\mathcal{W}$ is far less 'warped' than the input space $\mathcal{Z}$, so individual directions in $\mathcal{W}$ correspond to individual, interpretable attributes. That is what makes editing possible.

This walkthrough goes piece by piece: the mapping network and why $w$ beats $z$; how AdaIN injects style at each scale and gives coarse-vs-fine control; what the noise inputs do; and how style mixing both regularizes training and demonstrates the disentanglement.

Start with the problem. The input latent $z$ is, by construction, sampled from a fixed simple distribution — usually a standard Gaussian, a featureless round ball in, say, 512 dimensions. But the real data is not round. In the training images some attribute combinations are common (e.g. long hair) and others rare or absent. To map a round Gaussian onto that lumpy reality, a conventional generator has to warp and curve the latent space severely. In a warped space, moving in a straight line tangles several attributes together at once — that is entanglement.
StyleGAN inserts a step before the image is ever synthesized: a mapping network $f$, an 8-layer fully-connected MLP, that transforms the input code $z$ into an intermediate code $w$.

Reading it: $z$ is the raw Gaussian sample living in the input space $\mathcal{Z}$; $f$ is the learned 8-layer MLP; $w$ is the resulting intermediate latent in the space $\mathcal{W}$. Both are 512-dimensional. Nothing forces $\mathcal{W}$ to follow any fixed distribution — and that freedom is the whole point.

Why does this help? Because $\mathcal{W}$ is not pinned to a round Gaussian, the network can learn a mapping that unwarps the space: it can let the density of $w$ match the true density of attribute combinations, so the synthesis network downstream receives an already-disentangled code. The authors back this with two metrics they introduce — perceptual path length (how much the image changes per unit step in latent space; smoother is better) and linear separability (can a linear classifier read an attribute off the latent). Both show $\mathcal{W}$ is substantially more disentangled than $\mathcal{Z}$.

pages.title: Styles via AdaIN at Every Resolution
pages.subtitle: How w controls the image

blocks.html: Here is the architectural break with tradition. In a normal generator, $z$ is fed in only at the very bottom and everything flows up from there. StyleGAN does the opposite: the synthesis network $g$ starts from a fixed, learned constant tensor ($4\times4\times512$, the same for every image) and the latent $w$ is injected repeatedly, at every resolution, as a style.

The injection mechanism is AdaIN (Adaptive Instance Normalization, from the AdaIN paper in this collection). At each layer the feature map is first instance-normalized per channel, then re-scaled and re-shifted by style parameters derived from $w$:

Term by term: $x_i$ is feature channel $i$ of the current layer; $\mu(x_i)$ and $\sigma(x_i)$ are that channel's spatial mean and standard deviation, so $\tfrac{x_i-\mu(x_i)}{\sigma(x_i)}$ standardizes the channel to mean 0, variance 1 — erasing its existing 'style'. Then $y_{s,i}$ (a scale) and $y_{b,i}$ (a bias) re-impose a style. These $(y_s, y_b)$ are produced from $w$ by a learned affine layer $A$ — a different $A$ at each resolution — so each layer reads its own slice of style from the same $w$.

Why inject at every resolution? Because resolution maps to scale of feature. AdaIN at the coarse $4\times4$ to $8\times8$ layers controls high-level structure: pose, face shape, hairstyle, glasses. At the middle $16\times16$ to $32\times32$ layers it controls mid-level features: finer facial features, hair detail, eyes open or closed. At the fine $64\times64$ to $1024\times1024$ layers it controls colour scheme and micro-texture. Splitting style by scale is exactly what enables coarse-vs-fine control.

There is a subtle but important consequence of normalizing first: each AdaIN resets the per-channel statistics before applying the new style, so the effect of $w$ at a given layer is localized to that layer — one style does not leak uncontrollably into the next. This locality is part of why the styles at different scales stay separable.

Note the lineage: this is the AdaIN operation lifted out of style transfer and repurposed. In AdaIN the scale/shift were copied from a style image; here they are learned functions of $w$. Same math, new job — turning a latent code into controllable image style.

pages.title: Stochastic Noise
pages.subtitle: Where the random details come from

blocks.html: A real face has countless tiny details that are essentially random: the exact placement of each strand of hair, freckles, skin pores, the precise way stubble falls. These do not change who the person is — they are stochastic. Forcing the latent $w$ to encode all of them would waste capacity and entangle identity with noise. StyleGAN instead supplies randomness directly.

After each convolution, the network adds an explicit per-pixel Gaussian noise image, scaled by a learned per-channel factor, $x \leftarrow x + B\cdot n$, where $n$ is fresh single-channel Gaussian noise broadcast over channels and $B$ is a learned per-channel scaling weight. Because the noise is added at each resolution, coarse-layer noise affects large stochastic structure (broad hair flow) and fine-layer noise affects tiny detail (individual strands). Re-sampling only the noise, with $w$ fixed, changes these details while leaving identity, pose and overall look completely unchanged — a clean demonstration that the architecture has separated 'what the face is' (carried by $w$) from 'incidental texture' (carried by noise).

Because style enters at every resolution, you can feed different $w$ vectors to different ranges of layers — this is style mixing. Generate two codes $w_1$ and $w_2$ from two random $z$ vectors; use $w_1$ for the coarse layers and switch to $w_2$ for the fine layers (or vice versa). The result inherits coarse attributes (pose, face shape) from image 1 and fine attributes (colours, micro-texture) from image 2.

This is more than a party trick — it is also a regularizer applied during training. By randomly using two latents for two random layer ranges in a fraction of training batches, the network is discouraged from assuming adjacent layers' styles are correlated. That pressure forces each scale's style to stand on its own, sharpening the disentanglement and the scale-localized control.

The authors quantify quality with FID (Fréchet Inception Distance — lower is better; it compares the feature-space statistics of generated vs real images). Starting from a strong Progressive-GAN baseline, each addition stacks an improvement:

(FID figures are on the FFHQ face dataset, which the authors introduced alongside the model — 70,000 high-quality 1024x1024 faces. The trend is what matters: the style-based components drive the big drop from the baseline.)

Two metrics they introduced make the disentanglement claim measurable. Perceptual path length sums the perceptual change of the image as you interpolate through latent space — a smoother, shorter path means attributes vary gradually rather than lurching, a sign of disentanglement. Linear separability trains a linear classifier to read a binary attribute (e.g. gender) from the latent; if a single linear direction suffices, the attribute is cleanly encoded. On both, $\mathcal{W}$ beats $\mathcal{Z}$, confirming the mapping network does what it was designed to.

items: Leave the discriminator and loss alone; redesign only how the generator uses its latent code.
An 8-layer mapping network turns Gaussian $z$ into a disentangled $w$, unwarping the latent space.
$w$ is injected as AdaIN style at every resolution: coarse layers set pose and shape, fine layers set colour and texture.
Explicit per-pixel noise supplies stochastic detail without touching identity.
Style mixing both regularizes training and lets you combine coarse attributes of one image with fine attributes of another.
Result: photorealistic 1024px faces with unprecedented, scale-separated control.
